reason: The sources provide over 15 distinct claims with multiple citations regarding the meteorite's history, the 1996 life controversy, and its unique chemical composition.
story: In 1984, meteorite hunters in Antarctica's Allan Hills discovered a four-pound rock that would spark a global debate. Known as ALH 84001, it was later identified as a rare piece of the Martian crust, formed 4.1 billion years ago when Mars likely had liquid water. After an asteroid impact blasted it into space 16 million years ago, the rock drifted through the solar system before landing in the Antarctic ice 13,000 years ago. In 1996, NASA scientists announced they had found microscopic structures resembling fossilized bacteria inside the rock. The discovery was so monumental that President Bill Clinton delivered a televised address about it. While the scientific community eventually concluded these 'fossils' were likely inorganic mineral formations, the rock remains a cornerstone of astrobiology, with new Martian organic molecules discovered in the specimen as recently as 2020.
angle: A four-billion-year-old rock from Mars was found in the Antarctic ice containing what looked like microscopic fossils—triggering a formal televised announcement to the nation by the President of the United States.

claims.claim: Meteorite ALH 84001 was found in the Allan Hills of Antarctica.
The meteorite was discovered in December 1984 by an American team.
It was ejected from Mars by an asteroid impact approximately 15 to 17 million years ago.
The meteorite landed on Earth approximately 13,000 years ago.
In 1996, NASA scientists led by David McKay announced the rock might contain evidence of Martian life.
President Bill Clinton gave a televised speech regarding the potential discovery of life in the meteorite.
The microscopic structures found in the rock measure between 20 and 100 nanometers in diameter.
The rock contains polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) concentrated near carbonate globules.
The meteorite contains magnetite crystals similar to those produced biologically on Earth.
Most scientists eventually rejected the biological origin of the structures in favor of inorganic explanations.
The rock was the first one collected during the 1984 ANSMET expedition.
The structures were compared to theoretical 'nanobacteria,' which are now generally considered non-living.

disputed: The exact ejection date from Mars (S1 says 17 million years ago, S3 says 16 million, S4 says 15 million; the script should say 'around 16 million years ago').

The origin of the organic matter (S1 and S4 suggest PAHs are indigenous while amino acids are contamination; S2 suggests most organic matter is terrestrial; the script should attribute this to ongoing debate).
The source crater on Mars (S1 mentions Eos Chasma as a non-conclusive candidate; S6 suggests the Tooting crater for other shergottites; the script should treat the exact origin as unknown).
